lead: Linear algebra and probability are the working languages of machine learning. Linear algebra packs one example into a vector and a table into a matrix, so a model becomes a short formula. Probability describes what is not known: noise, missing labels, and the chance that a new user behaves like an old one. Distributions describe patterns of values; the Gaussian is the default bell curve. These ideas appear when you scale features, read a correlation matrix, or write a likelihood. This chapter gives the minimum needed for the rest of the course.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for features and data terms, and school algebra.

blocks.text: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. A feature vector x = (x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>, …, x<sub>n</sub>) stores n measurements for one example, such as age, monthly income in rupees, and number of UPI payments. A matrix X stores many examples: one row per example, one column per feature. If X has m rows and n columns, its shape is m × n.

The dot product combines two vectors into one number. It measures alignment. If θ is the angle between a and b, the dot product is also ||a|| ||b|| cos θ. The norm ||a|| = √(a · a) is length; ||a||<sub>2</sub> is the Euclidean length. A perceptron score and a linear-regression prediction both start with a dot product.
a · b = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>i</sub> = ||a|| ||b|| cos θ
blocks.where: a and b are vectors of length n; a<sub>i</sub> and b<sub>i</sub> are their i-th entries; ||a|| is the Euclidean norm; θ is the angle between them.

blocks.text: Matrix multiplication composes linear maps: C = AB has C<sub>ij</sub> = Σ<sub>k</sub> A<sub>ik</sub>B<sub>kj</sub>. The transpose Aᵀ flips rows and columns. The inverse A<sup>−1</sup> satisfies A<sup>−1</sup>A = I when A is square and full rank; many data matrices are not invertible, so least squares or regularization is used. Eigenvalues λ satisfy Av = λv for a nonzero vector v; PCA later uses them to find directions of largest variance.

A random variable maps an outcome to a number. A discrete random variable takes separate values, such as number of purchases (0, 1, 2, …). A continuous random variable takes any value in an interval, such as delivery time in minutes. P(A) is the probability of event A, a number from 0 to 1. P(A and B) is joint probability. P(A) alone is marginal probability. Conditional probability asks about one event given another.

blocks.where: P(B|A) is the conditional probability of B given A; P(A and B) is the joint probability of both events; P(A) is the marginal probability of A, with P(A) > 0.

blocks.text: Expectation E[X] is the long-run average. Variance Var(X) = E[(X−μ)²] is spread, with μ = E[X]. Its square root is standard deviation. Covariance Cov(X,Y) = E[(X−μ<sub>X</sub>)(Y−μ<sub>Y</sub>)] measures joint movement; correlation ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σ<sub>X</sub>σ<sub>Y</sub>) lies between −1 and 1 and has no units. Bayes rule rewrites P(A|B) using P(B|A); Unit 3 uses it for classifiers.
Independence means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(B|A) = P(B). It is not the same as zero correlation in general. The UPI example below shows the arithmetic.

Bernoulli(p) is one yes/no trial: P(1) = p, P(0) = 1−p, E[X] = p, Var(X) = p(1−p). Binomial(n,p) counts successes in n independent Bernoulli trials: P(X=k) = C(n,k)p<sup>k</sup>(1−p)<sup>n−k</sup>, where C(n,k) counts ways to choose k items from n. Uniform(a,b) gives equal density 1/(b−a) on [a,b]. The Gaussian (normal) N(μ,σ²) has a density set by its centre and spread.

blocks.where: f(x) is the density at x; μ is the mean; σ is the standard deviation; σ² is the variance; π ≈ 3.14159.

blocks.text: A multivariate Gaussian N(μ, Σ) has a mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ. Its shape is set by Σ: diagonal entries are variances, off-diagonal entries are covariances. The two curves in the figure have the same σ = 1 and different means. The density is not a probability at a point; area under the curve gives probability.

Before a model, look at each feature. Mean is the arithmetic average, sensitive to outliers. Median is the middle value after sorting, robust to outliers. IQR = Q3 − Q1 is the middle 50% spread; Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles. A histogram shows the shape of one variable; a box plot shows median, quartiles and possible outliers; a scatter plot shows two variables and hints at correlation.

Use these plots to find typos, missing values, heavy tails and engineering-unit mistakes. For example, a delivery-time column in seconds instead of minutes shows as a faraway cluster. Do not delete an outlier without a reason: it may be the rare fraud case you need. Correlation describes linear association only; a curved relation can have ρ near 0. See Unit 4 for feature selection and correlation analysis.

figure.caption: Two Gaussian densities with σ = 1: centre 0 and centre 1. The curves have the same spread; only the mean shifts them.

spec.aria: Two bell-shaped Gaussian density curves, one centered at 0 and one centered at 1.

examples.question: Among 1000 users, A means uses UPI and B means shops online. Counts: 400 use both, 200 use UPI only, 100 shop online only, and 300 neither. Find P(A), P(B), P(A and B) and P(B|A). Are A and B independent?
steps: P(B|A) = P(A and B)/P(A) = 0.40/0.60 = 400/600 = 0.667, rounded to three decimals.
Independence needs P(B|A) = P(B). Here 0.667 ≠ 0.50, so A and B are not independent.
examples.answer: P(A) = 0.60, P(B) = 0.50, P(A and B) = 0.40, P(B|A) = 0.667; A and B are not independent.
examples.check:
both = 400
upi_only = 200
online_only = 100
neither = 300
total = both + upi_only + online_only + neither
pA = (both + upi_only) / total
pB = (both + online_only) / total
pAB = both / total
pBA = both / (both + upi_only)
print(round(pA, 3))
print(round(pB, 3))
print(round(pAB, 3))
print(round(pBA, 3))

traps: P(A|B) and P(B|A) swap the conditioning event; use the denominator of the event that is given.
Variance has squared units; standard deviation returns to the original units.
Zero correlation means no linear association, not independence; independence implies zero covariance, but the reverse fails in general.
A density can exceed 1 for a narrow continuous variable; it is not a probability.
For skewed income data, mean is pulled by large values while median stays near the middle.

quiz.q: Define a feature vector and state the shape of a data matrix with m examples and n features.
quiz.a: A feature vector is an ordered list of n numbers for one example. The matrix shape is m × n: m rows, n columns.

quiz.q: Why is P(B|A) not the same as P(A|B) in general?
quiz.a: Each conditions on a different event, so each divides by a different marginal probability. P(B|A) divides by P(A), while P(A|B) divides by P(B).

quiz.q: For Bernoulli(p) with p = 0.2, find E[X] and Var(X).
For a Gaussian with μ = 0 and σ = 1, find the density at x = 0.
A scatter plot shows a clear U-shape but correlation ρ = 0.02. What do you conclude?
quiz.a: There is little linear association, but the variables are dependent. Correlation misses the curved relation, so inspect the plot and consider a nonlinear model.

quiz.q: Why is IQR often better than range for spotting outliers?
quiz.a: Range uses only the smallest and largest values, so one extreme value changes it. IQR uses Q1 and Q3 and ignores the extreme tails, so it is robust.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same ideas appear as NumPy arrays, pandas summary tables and correlation matrices. Probabilistic programming tools express models directly with distributions, and numerical linear algebra libraries solve large matrix problems. Search for covariance matrix, multivariate Gaussian, eigenvalue decomposition and exploratory data analysis to go deeper.
